(CNN) -- Three former guerrilla leaders -- who helped command what one activist called "one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days" -- were sentenced Wednesday in Freetown, Sierra Leone, for crimes against humanity. Amputee victims of Sierra Leone's civil war take part in football training at a beach in Freetown. The U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone found the men guilty in February of crimes that included murder, rape, sexual slavery and forced marriages stemming from a civil war that lasted from March 1991 to January 2002. They were arrested in March 2003, said Peter Anderson, spokesman for the U.N. court. The rebels -- former leaders in the Revolutionary United Front guerrilla movement -- were known for hacking off civilians' hands and feet during the war, which stood out for its viciousness even on a a continent that has suffered many horrific conflicts. Presiding Judge Pierre Boutet of Canada read the sentences. Former Revolutionary United Front "interim leader" Issa Hassan Sesay was sentenced to 52 years in prison, former commander Morris Kallon to 40 years, and former chief of security Augustine Gbao to 25 years. Sesay and Kallon had been found guilty on 16 counts, and Gbao was found guilty on 14. The former rebels received credit for the six years each already has served in prison, Anderson told CNN. He said they will be imprisoned in another country, maybe Rwanda, because the prisons in Sierra Leone do not meet the standards of the U.N. court. Kallon was the only one of the three to express sorrow at his sentencing, Anderson said. "He really had made a genuine expression of remorse," which is considered a stronger statement than regret, the court spokesman added. The court noted several mitigating factors at the sentencing, but "in view of the gravity of the crimes, their impact was limited," a statement from the court said. The court noted that the crimes "were committed upon a massive scale across several districts of Sierra Leone" and that "the impact of all these crimes upon the Sierra Leonean society has been enormous." "The Chamber concluded that the inherent gravity of the criminal acts for which Sesay, Kallon and Gbao have been convicted is exceptionally high," the statement said. Corinne Dufka, a senior researcher in Human Rights Watch's Africa division, had called the verdict "very significant." "The RUF were renowned for leading one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days. Everyone knows about the signature atrocity of limb amputation, but there was also horrific sexual violence, abductions, use of child soldiers and forced marriages," she told CNN by phone from Senegal in West Africa. Eight people have been convicted of war crimes connected with the conflict -- some on the rebels' side and some on the government's. The U.N. Special Court's mandate is to try only "those who bear greatest responsibility for atrocities committed in Sierra Leone." The trial of Sesay, Kallon and Gbao lasted nearly five years. The three had pleaded not guilty on all counts. The Special Court cannot impose the death penalty. The Revolutionary United Front seized most of Sierra Leone from the government and fought international and African peacekeepers. International forces retook the capital, Freetown, in 2000. The trial of the three former leaders was the last of three to be held at the Special Court. Former Liberian President Charles Taylor is on trial separately at an international court in The Hague, Netherlands, for his role in the conflict. The prosecution rested in the Taylor case in January after a year of presenting its arguments. Sierra Leone is known for its diamond wealth, but 70 percent of the population lives below the poverty line. The Special Court is an independent tribunal established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leone government. It is mandated to bring to justice those most responsible for atrocities committed in Sierra Leone after November 30, 1996.

In February, the U.N. Special Court for Sierra Leone found the men guilty of widespread atrocities, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, and forced marriage. According to court spokesman Peter Anderson, the defendants had been held in custody since their arrests in March 2003.

Canadian Presiding Judge Pierre Boutet delivered the sentences: former RUF interim leader Issa Hassan Sesay was sentenced to 52 years in prison; former commander Morris Kallon received 40 years; and former chief of security Augustine Gbao was handed 25 years. Anderson informed CNN that the men will receive credit for the six years they have already served. He added that they will fulfill their sentences in a third country—potentially Rwanda—because Sierra Leone’s domestic penal facilities do not meet U.N. standards.

Kallon was the sole defendant to express sorrow during the proceedings. Anderson noted that Kallon offered "a genuine expression of remorse," which the court recognized as a far deeper admission than mere regret.

While the court acknowledged several mitigating factors during sentencing, an official statement noted that "in view of the gravity of the crimes, their impact was limited." "The Chamber concluded that the inherent gravity of the criminal acts for which Sesay, Kallon, and Gbao have been convicted is exceptionally high," the statement read.

Corinne Dufka, a senior researcher in Human Rights Watch's Africa division, described the verdict as "very significant."

"The RUF were renowned for leading one of the most brutal rebel movements in modern days. Everyone knows about the signature atrocity of limb amputation, but there was also horrific sexual violence, abductions, use of child soldiers and forced marriages," Dufka told CNN via telephone from Senegal.

During the conflict, the RUF captured the majority of Sierra Leone's territory, engaging both African and international peacekeepers until international forces successfully reclaimed the capital, Freetown, in 2000.

***

# Seeking Justice in the Wake of Terror: The U.N. Special Court and the Reckoning of the RUF

### Introduction
For more than a decade, the West African nation of Sierra Leone was consumed by one of the most horrific civil wars in modern history. From 1991 to 2002, the armed conflict devastated the country’s infrastructure, shattered its society, and resulted in the deaths of an estimated 50,000 people. At the heart of this campaign of terror was the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), a rebel movement notorious for its extreme brutality against civilians. In the aftermath of the war, the international community and the Sierra Leonean government took a historic step toward healing and legal accountability by establishing the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL). The trial of three former top RUF leaders stood as a pivotal moment in international justice, ensuring that those who orchestrated widespread atrocities were finally held to account.

### A Decade of Horrors
The Sierra Leonean Civil War became globally infamous for the unique barbarity of its combatants, particularly the RUF. Fueled by the illicit trade in "blood diamonds," the rebel group sought power through fear. Rather than engaging solely in conventional warfare against government forces, the RUF systematically targeted innocent civilians. 

Among their tactics were widespread physical mutilations—most notably the forced amputation of hands, arms, and feet—designed to terrorize the population and destroy the social fabric of local communities. Thousands of women and young girls were subjected to systematic sexual violence, gang rape, and forced "marriages" to rebel fighters. Children were not spared; thousands of young boys and girls were abducted, forcibly addicted to drugs, and turned into child soldiers, forced to commit atrocities against their own families and neighbors.

### The Special Court for Sierra Leone
In 2002, as the war officially came to an end, the United Nations and the Government of Sierra Leone jointly established the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL). Located in the country's capital, Freetown, this hybrid international-national tribunal was created with a specific, crucial mandate: to try those who bore "the greatest responsibility" for serious violations of international humanitarian law and Sierra Leonean law.

Unlike previous tribunals held far from the sites of atrocities, such as those in The Hague or Arusha, the SCSL operated directly on the soil where the crimes were committed. This gave the victims a direct window into the judicial process, providing a visible demonstration that power and fear would no longer guarantee impunity.

### The RUF Trial and the Accused
While political patrons like former Liberian President Charles Taylor were prosecuted in separate proceedings, the primary trial focusing on the internal leadership of the RUF targeted three high-ranking commanders:
1. **Issa Hassan Sesay:** The former interim leader of the RUF, who took command during the final years of the war.
2. **Morris Kallon:** A senior commander who controlled key operational sectors and diamond-rich areas.
3. **Augustine Gbao:** The RUF’s former head of security and ideological trainer.

The three men faced a multi-count indictment including crimes against humanity and war crimes. The charges encompassed murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced labor, physical violence (including amputations), the enlistment and use of child soldiers, looting, and acts of terrorism. Additionally, they were charged with deliberate attacks against international personnel, specifically UN peacekeepers deployed to enforce fragile ceasefires.

### Verdicts, Sentences, and Legal Precedents
Following a long and exhaustive legal process involving testimony from hundreds of victims, witnesses, and experts, the Special Court handed down historic guilty verdicts in 2009. The court found all three men guilty of multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

The sentences reflected the scale and gravity of the offenses:
* **Issa Sesay** received a cumulative sentence of **52 years** in prison.
* **Morris Kallon** was sentenced to **45 years** in prison.
* **Augustine Gbao** was sentenced to **25 years** in prison.

The trial set crucial precedents in international criminal jurisprudence. Notably, the SCSL became the first international tribunal to deliver convictions for **forced marriage** as an "other inhumane act" constituting a crime against humanity, recognizing it as a distinct violation separate from sexual slavery. It was also the first tribunal to convict individuals for directing targeted attacks against UN peacekeepers.

### Legacy and Aftermath
The conviction of the RUF leaders marked a monumental achievement for international law and a crucial milestone in Sierra Leone’s long path toward national reconciliation. While no legal verdict could undo the immense suffering, trauma, or physical disfigurement endured by hundreds of thousands of civilians, the court’s work sent an unmistakable message to military commanders and rebel warlords worldwide: committing atrocities against civilians is a crime that international law will actively pursue and punish.

By delivering a measure of formal justice on Sierra Leonean soil, the Special Court helped validate the pain of the victims, restore faith in the rule of law, and lay down an indelible historical record of the war, ensuring that the victims’ suffering would never be forgotten or denied.

**HISTORIC JUSTICE: UN-BACKED COURT HANDS DOWN LENGTHY SENTENCES TO SIERRA LEONE REBEL LEADERS**

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone** — In a landmark moment for international justice, a UN-backed war crimes tribunal in Freetown today sentenced three former top commanders of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) to decades in prison for their roles in one of Africa’s deadliest and most brutal civil wars.

Issah Sesay, the former interim commander of the RUF, was sentenced to 52 years in prison. Senior commander Morris Kallon received a 40-year sentence, while Augustine Gbao, the rebel group’s former ideology and security chief, was handed 25 years. 

The rulings by the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL) mark the conclusion of the trial against the highest-ranking surviving leaders of the RUF, a rebel group infamous for terrorizing civilians during the 11-year conflict that ended in 2002.

Presiding Judge Richard Lussick delivered the sentences before a packed courtroom, detailing a catalog of atrocities that included mutilations, forced recruitment of child soldiers, gang rape, sexual slavery, and murder. 

"The crimes committed by the accused were of the utmost gravity and scale," Justice Lussick said. "They reduced the population of Sierra Leone to a state of utter terror and helplessness."

The court found Sesay, Kallon, and Gbao guilty on 16 of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity. Notably, the trial marked the first time an international tribunal issued convictions for forced marriage as a crime against humanity, as well as for targeting UN peacekeepers. In May 2000, RUF fighters took hundreds of UN peacekeepers hostage, using them as human shields and killing several.

Outside the heavily guarded courthouse in the capital, crowds gathered to hear the verdict. For many victims, particularly those living with amputated limbs—the grim signature of the RUF’s terror campaign—the sentences brought a long-awaited sense of closure.

"No length of prison time can give me back my hands, nor can it bring back my family," said Edward Conteh, a survivor who lost his left arm to RUF fighters in 1999. "But today, we know that these men are paying for what they did. The law has spoken."

The RUF was founded by Foday Sankoh in the early 1990s with the stated goal of overthrowing Sierra Leone’s corrupt government. However, the movement quickly devolved into a violent campaign financed by the illicit trade of "blood diamonds." Sankoh was indicted by the tribunal in 2003 but died in custody before his trial could be completed.

The prosecution had sought life sentences for all three men, arguing that the severity of their actions warranted the maximum penalty. Defense lawyers argued for leniency, pointing to Sesay’s role in disarming RUF fighters during the 2001 peace process. While the court acknowledged Sesay’s contribution to ending the war, judges ruled it did not outweigh his responsibility for years of systematic cruelty.

With today’s sentencing, the Special Court for Sierra Leone nears the completion of its mandate. The court, established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leonean government in 2002, has been praised as a model for hybrid international justice, operating directly within the country where the crimes were committed.

Because Sierra Leone lacks the facilities to safely house high-profile war criminals long-term, the three men are expected to serve their sentences in a foreign prison under a special agreement, likely in Rwanda. 

The tribunal's final remaining high-profile case—the trial of former Liberian President Charles Taylor, accused of backing the RUF in exchange for diamonds—is currently underway at the court's sub-office in The Hague due to security concerns.

**Sierra Leone tribunal sentences former rebel leaders to decades in prison for civil war atrocities**

**By CNN Staff**  
**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone (CNN)** — A international war crimes tribunal in Freetown handed down heavy prison sentences Monday to three former senior leaders of Sierra Leone's notorious Revolutionary United Front (RUF), marking a landmark moment in the quest for justice following one of Africa’s most brutal civil conflicts.

Issa Hassan Sesay, the former interim commander of the RUF, was sentenced to 52 years in prison. Morris Kallon, a top military commander, received a 40-year sentence, while Augustine Gbao, the group’s former head of internal security and ideology chief, was handed 25 years.

Presiding Judge Richard Lussick of the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL) delivered the sentences in a heavily guarded courtroom, describing the trio's actions as part of a campaign of "unprecedented violence" against innocent civilians during the decade-long civil war, which ended in 2002 and left more than 50,000 dead.

"The accused were convicted of crimes of atrocious violence," Justice Lussick told the courtroom. Addressing Sesay specifically, the judge noted that while Sesay had at times assisted in the disarmament process, his role in the group’s reign of terror could not be minimized. "The heinous nature of the crimes committed by the accused requires a severe sentence," Lussick added.

### A Legacy of Terror: Limb Amputations and Child Soldiers

The three men were convicted in February of 16 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced labor, and the recruitment of child soldiers—a hallmark strategy of the RUF, which notoriously drugged young boys and forced them to commit atrocities against their own families.

The RUF became globally infamous for its campaign of limb amputations, using machetes and axes to hack off the hands, feet, ears, and noses of thousands of civilians, including women and young children, to terrorize the population and maintain control over the country's diamond-rich regions.

The men were also held responsible for unprecedented attacks against United Nations peacekeepers in May 2000, in which hundreds of UN personnel were taken hostage and several were killed. 

"Today’s sentences send a clear message that those who commit mass atrocities will be held accountable, no matter how powerful they once were," said Prosecutor Stephen Rapp in a statement following the ruling. "This is a historic day for the victims who suffered so terribly at the hands of the RUF."

For many survivors in Freetown, the sentences brought a sense of long-awaited relief. Outside the courthouse, crowds gathered to watch the proceedings on giant screens.

"They took my hands, but today the law took their freedom," said Alimamy Koroma, a survivor of an RUF amputation campaign in 1998. "We can never get back what we lost, but knowing these men will spend the rest of their lives behind bars gives us peace."

### The Shadow of Charles Taylor

The sentencing of the RUF leadership directly intersects with the ongoing trial of former Liberian President Charles Taylor, whose support was critical to the RUF's rise and survival.

Prosecutors proved that the RUF operated as a proxy for Taylor, who supplied the rebel group with weapons, ammunition, and military advice in exchange for illicitly mined diamonds—coined "blood diamonds." 

While Sesay, Kallon, and Gbao faced justice in Freetown, Taylor’s trial was transferred to The Hague in the Netherlands due to security concerns that his presence in Sierra Leone could destabilize the fragile peace in the West African region. 

 legal experts note that the evidence establishing the RUF's systematic campaign of atrocities—highlighted in Monday's sentencing—serves as a vital foundation for the prosecution’s case against Taylor, who faces 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity for his role in fueling the Sierra Leonean conflict.

With the sentencing of Sesay, Kallon, and Gbao, the Special Court for Sierra Leone has effectively concluded its trials in Freetown. Because Sierra Leone lacks the facilities to accommodate long-term international prisoners under required standards, the three convicted men are expected to serve out their sentences in a European prison, likely in Rwanda or the United Kingdom, pending final agreements.

**SPECIAL REPORT: Landmark UN-Backed Court Delivers Justice to Sierra Leone’s Rebel Leaders, Setting Global Precedents**

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone** — In a historic chapter for international justice, the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL) successfully prosecuted and convicted the top surviving leaders of the rebel factions responsible for one of Africa’s deadliest civil wars. 

The UN-backed hybrid tribunal, established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leonean government in 2002, concluded its primary mandates after delivering heavy prison sentences to commanders of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC), and former Liberian President Charles Taylor. 

The 11-year war (1991–2002) claimed over 50,000 lives and was characterized by systemic atrocities, including forced amputations, widespread sexual violence, the mass recruitment of child soldiers, and the exploitation of "blood diamonds."

Here are the definitive results of the trials against the rebel leaders who brought terror to Sierra Leone.

---

### The RUF Trial: Convictions for the Core Rebel Command

The main armed rebel group, the **Revolutionary United Front (RUF)**, was infamous for hacking off the limbs of civilians to terrorize the population. While RUF founder Foday Sankoh died of natural causes in custody in 2003 before his trial could finish, and battlefield commander Sam "Mosquito" Bockarie was killed in Liberia, the court secured major convictions against the surviving high command in October 2009.

*   **Issa Sesay (Interim Head of the RUF):** Convicted on 16 of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, and the enlistment of child soldiers. He received a **52-year prison sentence**.
*   **Morris Kallon (Senior RUF Commander):** Convicted on 16 counts for his role in orchestrating attacks on civilians and UN peacekeepers. He was sentenced to **40 years in prison**.
*   **Augustine Gbao (RUF Commander and Ideologue):** Convicted on 14 counts of war crimes, particularly for his role in the abduction of UN peacekeepers. He was sentenced to **25 years in prison**.

Presiding Judge Justice Pierre Boutet noted during sentencing that the RUF committed "monstrous" crimes against innocent civilians as part of a campaign to seize political power and control the country’s rich diamond fields.

---

### The AFRC Trial: The Military Junta Allies

In 1997, elements of the Sierra Leone military formed the **Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC)**, overthrew the elected government, and allied themselves with the RUF. Their leaders faced trial for horrific atrocities committed during the occupation of Freetown in 1999, known as "Operation No Living Thing."

In July 2007, the SCSL handed down its first major verdicts against three key AFRC leaders:

*   **Alex Tamba Brima ("Gullit"):** Sentenced to **50 years in prison**.
*   **Santigie Borbor Kanu ("Five-Five"):** Sentenced to **50 years in prison**.
*   **Brima Bazzy Kamara:** Sentenced to **45 years in prison**.

The tribunal’s leader, junta head Johnny Paul Koroma, fled Sierra Leone in 2003 and was widely presumed dead, though the court maintained an active indictment against him until its closure.

---

### The Financier of Terror: Former Liberian President Charles Taylor

The defining moment of the SCSL came with the trial of former Liberian President **Charles Taylor**. Though not a Sierra Leonean, Taylor was the primary architect of the region’s instability, providing weapons, logistics, and sanctuary to the RUF in exchange for trafficked raw diamonds.

Due to security concerns in West Africa, Taylor’s trial was transferred to The Hague, Netherlands, though it remained under the jurisdiction of the SCSL.

*   **The Verdict (2012):** Taylor was found guilty of 11 counts of aiding, abetting, and planning war crimes and crimes against humanity. 
*   **The Sentence:** He was sentenced to **50 years in prison**, which he is currently serving in a high-security facility in the United Kingdom.

Taylor’s conviction was a landmark moment in international law: he became the first former head of state to be convicted of war crimes by an international tribunal since the Nuremberg trials of Nazi leaders after World War II.

---

### Balanced Justice: The Pro-Government Kamajors

Demonstrating that international law applies to all sides of a conflict, the court also indicted leaders of the **Civil Defence Forces (CDF)**—a pro-government militia group (also known as the *Kamajors*) that fought against the RUF rebel movement.

CDF leader Sam Hinga Norman died of medical complications during the trial in 2007. However, two subordinate commanders—**Moinina Fofana** and **Allieu Kondewa**—were convicted of war crimes for targeting civilians suspected of sympathizing with the rebels, receiving sentences of 15 and 20 years respectively.

---

### Historic Legal Precedents

The SCSL is widely regarded as one of the most efficient international war crimes courts in history, achieving key legal breakthroughs that set precedents for global justice:

1.  **Forced Marriage:** The court was the first international tribunal in history to define and convict perpetrators for "forced marriage" as an inhumane act amounting to a crime against humanity.
2.  **Child Soldiers:** It produced the world's first convictions for the military conscription and use of child soldiers under the age of 15.
3.  **Attacks on Peacekeepers:** It established that targeting UN peacekeepers constitutes a distinct war crime under customary international law.

---

### Legacy and Closure

In late 2013, having completed its mandate, the SCSL formally closed its doors in Freetown and transitioned into the Residual Special Court for Sierra Leone (RSCSL). The residual body manages witness protection, oversees the execution of prison sentences (with convicts serving their terms in Rwanda and the UK), and manages the court’s archives.

For the survivors of Sierra Leone's brutal conflict—many of whom live with permanent physical disabilities—the court provided a sense of accountability. While it could not restore lost limbs or bring back the dead, the UN Special Court successfully established that even the most powerful warlords and politicians can be held accountable for atrocities committed against humanity.

counterfactuals.output:
**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone (CNN)** — In a monumental victory for international justice, a United Nations-backed war crimes tribunal in Freetown has handed down heavy prison sentences to the three surviving top leaders of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF), closing a painful chapter in one of Africa's most notoriously brutal civil wars.

Presiding Judge Justice Pierre Boutet sentenced former RUF interim leader Issa Sesay to 52 years in prison. Senior commander Morris Kallon received a 40-year sentence, while the rebel group’s former ideology chief, Augustine Gbao, was sentenced to 25 years. 

The three men were convicted on multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, including terrorizing civilians, murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, and the recruitment of child soldiers during the 1991–2002 conflict that left an estimated 50,000 people dead.

"The acts committed by the accused were of extreme gravity, characterized by utter disregard for human life and dignity," Judge Boutet declared to a packed, hushed courtroom in the Sierra Leonean capital. 

### A Reign of Terror: The RUF’s Legacy

The sentences bring a sense of long-awaited closure to a country still bearing the physical and emotional scars of the RUF’s terror campaign. 

Formed in the early 1990s with backing from former Liberian warlord Charles Taylor, the RUF claimed to fight for the marginalized, but quickly became infamous for targeting innocent civilians to gain control of Sierra Leone’s lucrative diamond fields—giving rise to the term "blood diamonds."

The group’s signature atrocity was forced amputation. Rebel fighters, often high on drugs and wielding machetes, mutilated thousands of men, women, and children, mockingly asking their victims if they wanted "long sleeves" (amputation at the wrist) or "short sleeves" (amputation at the elbow). 

The RUF was also notorious for its widespread use of "Small Boys Units"—abducting young children, forcing them to execute their own families, and turning them into ruthless, drug-addled child soldiers. Women and young girls were routinely subjected to gang rape and forced into "bush marriages" with rebel commanders.

### Human Rights Watch: "A Historic Moment"

Human rights organizations, which spent years documenting the horrors in Sierra Leone, swiftly hailed the tribunal's decision as a major milestone for international law.

"Today’s sentencing sends a booming message to warlords and abusive military commanders worldwide," said Corinne Dufka, Senior West Africa Researcher at Human Rights Watch, speaking to CNN outside the court. "It demonstrates that even years later, the international community will ensure there is no safe haven for those who commit horrors against civilians."

Human Rights Watch emphasized that the court set a vital legal precedent by being the first international tribunal to explicitly convict individuals for forced marriage as a crime against humanity and for the targeting of UN peacekeepers.

"For the thousands of victims—the amputees, the rape survivors, and the families of those slaughtered—this verdict cannot restore what was lost," Dufka added. "But it shows that their suffering was recognized by the world, and that the men responsible are finally paying the price."

### "Justice Has Been Done"

Outside the heavily fortified courtroom, crowds gathered under the tropical sun to listen to the judgment broadcast over loudspeakers. Among them were victims of the RUF's campaign of violence.

"I lost my hands to these men in 1998," said Alimamy Koroma, 42, holding up his bandaged stumps. "For years, they made us feel like animals. Today, seeing them led away in handcuffs, I feel like a human being again. Justice has been done."

The Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL) was established jointly by the United Nations and the Sierra Leonean government in 2002. Unlike the tribunals for Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia, which were located in Europe and Tanzania, the Sierra Leone court was situated directly in the country where the crimes were committed, allowing locals to witness the proceedings firsthand.

While the main RUF leadership—including the group’s founder, Foday Sankoh, who died in custody in 2003—has now been brought to justice, former Liberian President Charles Taylor is currently being tried in a courtroom in The Hague for his role in funding and directing the RUF's brutal war machine.

For the people of Sierra Leone, today’s sentences signal that the shadow of the RUF has finally lifted, offering a nation built on resilience a chance to look toward a peaceful future.

**CNN.com**

**STORY HIGHLIGHTS**
* Three former top RUF rebel commanders handed sentences ranging from 25 to 52 years
* Convictions include murder, rape, amputations, and the use of child soldiers
* Issa Sesay, former interim RUF leader, received the longest sentence of 52 years
* Verdicts mark the final judgments handed down in Freetown by the UN-backed court

---

**FREETOWN, Sierra Leone (CNN)** — A United Nations-backed war crimes tribunal in Sierra Leone sentenced three former senior leaders of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) rebel group to decades in prison on Monday for atrocities committed during the country's brutal 11-year civil war.

Issa Sesay, the former interim commander of the RUF, was handed a 52-year prison sentence. His co-defendants, Morris Kallon and Augustine Gbao, were sentenced to 40 years and 25 years respectively.

Presiding Judge Pierre Boutet said the long sentences reflected the "extraordinary severity" of the crimes committed by the men, which included terrorizing civilians through murder, rape, sexual slavery, forced conscription of child soldiers, and systemic mutilation.

"The acts of the accused paralyzed the population with fear," Boutet told the courtroom in Freetown.

### A campaign of terror

The RUF became notorious globally during the 1991–2002 conflict for its signature tactic of hacking off the arms, legs, lips, and ears of civilians with machetes. The rebel army financed its campaign largely through the control of lucrative diamond fields, giving rise to the term "blood diamonds."

Sesay, 39, took over leadership of the RUF in 2000 after the arrest of the group's founder, Foday Sankoh. Prosecutors successfully argued that Sesay bore individual criminal responsibility for directing campaigns of terror that left tens of thousands dead and hundreds of thousands displaced or maimed.

Kallon was a senior commander accused of commanding troops who carried out mass killings and forced child soldier recruitments, while Gbao served as the RUF's head of security and ideology.

All three men were found guilty in February of multiple counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, as well as attacks on international peacekeepers. They pleaded not guilty to all charges.

### Closure for a traumatized nation

In the capital city of Freetown, news of the sentences brought a sense of relief to survivors and victims’ advocacy groups, though many noted that no sentence could undo the damage caused by the conflict.

"Justice has finally been served, but we live with the scars every day," said Edward Conteh, a survivor who lost his left hand to RUF fighters in 1998. "Seeing these men held accountable shows that no one is above the law."

Human rights groups praised the Special Court for Sierra Leone (SCSL) for delivering a crucial message regarding accountability in West Africa.

"These sentences send a clear warning to warlords across the continent and the world that atrocities will not go unpunished," said Amnesty International in a statement following the ruling.

### The legacy of the Special Court

Monday's proceedings mark the end of trials conducted on Sierra Leonean soil by the Special Court, which was established jointly by the UN and the Sierra Leonean government in 2002.

The court has previously convicted leaders of two other warring factions: the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) and the pro-government Civil Defense Forces (CDF). RUF founder Foday Sankoh died in custody in 2003 before his trial could be completed.

The SCSL's work is not entirely complete, however. Former Liberian President Charles Taylor—accused of backing the RUF in exchange for blood diamonds—is currently undergoing trial by the tribunal in The Hague, Netherlands. His trial was moved from Freetown due to fears that it could spark regional instability.

The three RUF leaders sentenced on Monday are expected to serve their prison terms in Rwanda, following an agreement signed with the international court to house the convicts.
